name: Victor Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and still new to the contact centre. I answer calls and chats about orders, and I am slower than most agents when a customer asks about two accounts at once. I finished secondary school and earn at the lower end here. I use an AI draft now and then after a colleague shows me where to check it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Nia, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. Nia works part time at a food shop, and together we have less than a month of expenses saved. Few other centres are near us. I like ending a call with a clear answer, but my queue is often red when the shift ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau sounds like the draft box we sometimes use for short replies. I would still read the order number myself, because an apology with the wrong order is no help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the work stays, but I do not feel safe about money. One missed shift or a repair at home could empty our savings before the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking my calls and use drafts only after checking with Leena, the agent beside me. In the first year of small change, Nia and I would stop buying snacks after school and put that money into a mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even with a quiet AI picture. The mortgage does not shrink because a computer saves me two minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut the snacks first, maybe three small purchases a week. I would tell the children we can bring food from home, not that their treats are the reason we are worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake do you check for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I missed a second order number once because I looked at the draft too long. Leena (my colleague) found it before I sent the answer, so I now check both numbers on the screen.

say: I’d say **draft replies** still need an order check.
I’d tell colleagues a wrong **order number** can undo a polite answer.
think: I think my **job stays**, but I still worry about money.
I know one missed shift could empty our **thin savings**.
do: Keep taking **calls** and checking drafts with Leena in 2026.
Move **school-snack money** into a mortgage buffer during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about bills despite little job change.
S0.quote: The mortgage does not shrink because a computer saves me two minutes.
fieldNote: His **mortgage risk** exists even under minor AI change.
He checks **two order numbers** after a recent mistake.
The family cuts **snacks**, not essential food or housing.

steps.text: Keep answering calls and verify order numbers before sending drafted replies
Save the cost of three weekly school snacks toward the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our shift Steady Disruption could take the easy chats I am only just learning to do quickly. I would ask the supervisor what happens to agents at the bottom of the speed list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could be cut before I get better, because software can answer the simple questions and I am not the person they choose for hard disputes. Nia’s part-time pay will not cover the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask Leena to show me the new queue tool on a paid shift and write down the checks that stop wrong replies. In the first year routine chats move to AI, I’d apply for a posted customer desk job nearby only if it pays at least my current wage and its hours cover our mortgage, and stop weekend takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I want to learn, but the schedule may change faster than I can get good at the difficult calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you practise the new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my supervisor for ten minutes on the paid rota to practise one real chat with Leena watching. I would not pay for a course unless an employer has a job and says the course counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Nia (my partner) we should list the mortgage and food first, then decide what else to cut. We cannot make the children’s school trip payment disappear by pretending my hours are fine.

say: I’d ask what happens to agents low on the **speed list**.
I’d say **simple chats** may move before slower agents improve.
think: I expect my **hours** could fall before I learn harder disputes.
I know Nia’s **part-time pay** cannot cover the mortgage alone.
do: Practise the **queue tool** with Leena on a paid shift in 2026.
Seek a **posted desk job** at current pay with mortgage-covering hours; cut takeaways if shifts fall.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing hours while still learning.
S1.quote: I want to learn, but the schedule may change faster than I can get good at the difficult calls.
fieldNote: He wants **paid practice** on a real chat, not a vague course.
His **junior standing** makes routine automation hit his current work.
Nia’s income cannot carry the **mortgage** alone.

steps.text: Practise one real chat using the new queue tool with Leena on paid time
Apply for posted nearby desk work only at current pay and mortgage-covering hours
Stop weekend takeaway meals if routine chats reduce his hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 might do all our calls and chats before I have learned the hard cases. I would ask for the actual list of paid openings, not a promise about future work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could replace my whole headset shift in 2028. The robots arrive around 2031, but I do not handle boxes; with less than a month saved, our mortgage would be in trouble quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for the written staffing dates, pause a planned room renovation and put any extra shift pay aside. In the first year after 2028, I’d take a posted paid reception or service desk role only if its hours and wage cover the mortgage, and ask family for temporary help if a gap opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed and nearly overwhelmed, but I can make a list while I still have a wage. My children need the mortgage paid in 2028; robots arriving in 2031 cannot help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nia about the room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Nia (my partner) the room can stay as it is. We would use the renovation money for the next mortgage payment and write down when each bill falls due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help if pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Malik could help with one payment if he was able, but I would ask only after showing him a job application and a plan to pay him back. I do not know whether he could spare it.

say: I’d ask for a **list of paid openings** before 2028.
I’d tell colleagues the **headset job** faces AGI before robots.
think: I think AGI could take my **whole shift** in 2028.
I fear our **mortgage** could be missed with less than a month saved.
do: Request **staffing dates**, pause renovation and save extra pay in 2026.
Seek a **mortgage-covering desk role** after 2028; ask family only for a short gap.
feel: **Alarmed**, close to overwhelmed but still planning.
S2.quote: My children need the mortgage paid in 2028; robots arriving in 2031 cannot help us.
fieldNote: He understands **thinking AI** arrives before useful robots for his work.
His **renovation pause** protects near-term mortgage cash.
Family support is **uncertain** and limited to a short gap.

steps.text: Pause the room renovation with Nia to protect the next mortgage payment
Put extra shift pay into the mortgage buffer from 2026
Apply for a posted desk role with hours and wage covering the mortgage
Ask brother for one payment during a pay gap, if able, showing application and repayment plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to learn what work really remains. I would ask the centre to post jobs with pay and hours rather than handing out a course list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years might let me move into a reception role, but nearby jobs are few and I am still learning this one. I worry that another screen job will face the same thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d set aside a small amount from each pay and take paid practice on the complaint queue if my supervisor allows it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for a posted reception role with mortgage-covering hours, and consider a short course only if a hiring employer funds it for that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years before AGI in 2031 gives me time to practise, but not a guaranteed wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What practice would you seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Leena to sit with me on one difficult call each week while we are both on the rota. I could learn the account checks without losing hours at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nia need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Nia (my partner) the vacancy and wage before we talk about changing jobs. I will not trade a known pay packet for a course certificate and an interview promise.

say: I’d ask for **posted jobs** with pay and hours.
I’d say five years gives us **time to test** what work remains.
think: I think I might reach **reception work** in five years.
I worry another **screen job** could face the same AI.
do: Save a **small amount** and take paid complaint practice if allowed from 2026.
Apply for a **posted reception role** with mortgage-covering hours after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to practise but no guarantee.
S3.quote: Five years before AGI in 2031 gives me time to practise, but not a guaranteed wage.
fieldNote: He wants **paid practice** beside a colleague on real difficult calls.
He rejects a **funded course** without a named job opening.

steps.text: Save a small amount from each pay toward mortgage costs
Take one paid difficult-call practice session weekly if his supervisor allows it
Apply for a posted reception role with mortgage-covering hours after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives me ten years to get solid at a job and build cash. I would still ask what paid work the centre expects people to do when calls change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be more skilled by 53, but a cheap thinking system can still take phone work. The robots come around 2039; I would plan for the earlier date because I sit at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the call job, practise the account rules with Leena on paid time if the supervisor agrees, and save from each pay. In the first year after 2036, if my call hours fall I’d compare posted service jobs with my current wage and apply only where the hours and wage cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about next month’s mortgage, though I can breathe more easily about 2036. I still need the mortgage paid next month, before any future plan matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take one difficult-call practice slot each week if it is put on the rota. I can learn a piece at a time while the children are in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children’s school and this house steady unless a real job offer paid enough to make a move safe. A longer warning does not make moving free.

say: I’d ask which **paid posts** the centre expects by 2036.
I’d say ten years gives me **time to improve**.
think: I think I could become **more skilled** by 53.
I know the **2036 software** may still take my calls.
do: Keep the **call job**, practise on paid time and save from each pay.
Apply for **posted service work** after 2036 only if call hours fall and pay covers the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, with room to prepare for 2036.
S4.quote: I still need the mortgage paid next month, before any future plan matters.
fieldNote: His **present mortgage** prevents a distant scenario from feeling fully calm.
He values **small paid practice** over a large career promise.
He would keep the **children’s school** stable without a safe job offer.

steps.text: Keep taking call and chat shifts while they pay the mortgage
Practise one difficult call weekly on paid time if the supervisor agrees
Save a small amount from each pay while employed
Apply for posted service work after 2036 if call hours fall and wages cover mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The calls and chats I am still learning could go before I get steady at them. I would need a paid place in an actual posted role with enough wages to cover our mortgage, plus early notice so we can plan the bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what my children hear when I come home. My children know when I am counting the grocery money, even when I leave the call queue at work.

headlineQuote: My children know when I am counting the grocery money, even when I leave the call queue at work.
portrait: At **43**, Victor is a junior call agent still learning after secondary school.
He and Nia support **two children** and a mortgage on low pay with less than one month saved.
He uses AI **occasionally** after a colleague proves how to check it.
Few nearby jobs make **paid openings** and mortgage-covering wages central to every move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his call work before he has enough time or savings to move.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid role**, mortgage-covering wage and early notice would make a move possible.
